summary: Specifies a Telnet option for hosts that want to support the 3270 data stream inside Telnet. It was a proposed standard, and is now historic. It was updated by RFC 6270.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a Telnet option for negotiating use of the 3270 data stream. The client lists terminal types it supports, and the server selects one or chooses NVT ASCII.

questions: what is the telnet 3270 regime option
how to use 3270 terminals over telnet
how does telnet negotiate a 3270 terminal
subtitle: A Telnet option for agreeing on a 3270 terminal type and data mode.

tldr.problem: Using a 3270 data stream over Telnet required separate negotiations for terminal type, binary transmission, and end-of-record handling.
tldr.mechanism: The 3270-REGIME option lets a client list supported terminal types and lets the server select one, with binary data and an end-of-record delimiter implied by the regime.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Historic and is updated by RFC 6270.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1041 as Historic and updated by RFC 6270. RFC 1041 was published in January 1988 as a proposed standard.

sections.title: Why a 3270 Regime Option Was Proposed
sections.content:
A Telnet server running VM or MVS can use this option to agree with a client whether to exchange 3270 data or NVT ASCII. Earlier setup relied on three separate options: TERMINALTYPE, BINARY, and EOR. The order was unspecified, and it was unclear when the 3270 mode had actually begun.

The new option was intended to combine the agreement: both sides use eight-bit binary data, use IAC EOR as a delimiter, and agree on a terminal type. This RFC defines negotiation, not the 3270 data-stream protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier Telnet setup required several separate agreements before the computers could exchange 3270 data. This option was proposed to negotiate the terminal type and data mode together.

sections.title: The Terminal-Type List
sections.content:
The option is named 3270-REGIME and has code 29. After both sides permit the option, the client sends an ARE subnegotiation containing a list of supported terminal types. The server replies with an IS subnegotiation naming the selected type.

The list is an ASCII string with terminal type names separated by spaces. A name with an embedded space or backslash uses a backslash escape. An empty list means the sender supports only NVT ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a list of terminal types it can use. The server chooses a type from that list, or both sides can use NVT ASCII.

sections.title: Negotiation and Switching Modes
sections.content:
Both hosts exchange WILL and DO commands before sending subnegotiation. The client sends the list with ARE, and the server responds with the selected type using IS. The list is ordered from most to least desirable, so the server can select the first type it supports.

Sending an empty list switches the connection to NVT ASCII. When changing terminal type, the client can include both the current and new types so the server can keep the current type if it cannot use the new one. Each renegotiation repeats the full process.
sections.plainLanguage: The client lists its preferred terminal types first, and the server selects one it supports. An empty list requests NVT ASCII instead.

sections.title: Data Handling During Negotiation
sections.content:
The IAC character is also used in Telnet control sequences, so an IAC byte that is part of the 3270 data stream must be escaped by sending it twice. The RFC also recommends pausing user data while negotiation is under way so data is not confused with negotiation commands.

The server switches regimes after sending IS, and the client switches after receiving it. A change may require both sides to flush data already waiting to be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need to keep control commands separate from terminal data while they negotiate. They change modes only when the selection has been sent and received.
